newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seen bungling Thomson sale from start.
newsitem.headline: France seen bungling Thomson sale from start.

text.p: The French government's decision on Wednesday to pull the plug on the privatisation of electronics giant Thomson SA capped a botched nine-month effort that looked doomed from the start.

The government's biggest mistake, industry experts said, was its failure to gauge the visceral opposition in France to the proposed sale of Thomson's huge consumer electronics branch to a South Korean company.

Corporate chairmen, ministers and even Prime Minister Alain Juppe were wiping egg off their faces after France's independent Privatisation Commission refused to rubber-stamp the sale plan, obliging the government to scrap it.

The Finance Ministry said the commission's decision reflected reservations about selling Thomson Multimedia (TMM) to South Korea's Daewoo Electronics. The proposed sale raised an outcry in nationalistic France where South Korean companies are widely regarded as treating their workers poorly.

"This privatisation got off badly right from the start," said Elie Cohen, research director at the prestigious CNRS -- Conseil Nationale de Recherche Scientifique -- think-tank and an expert on French industrial policy.

President Jacques Chirac announced plans in February to sell Thomson under three conditions -- the buyer would be French, it would not break up the group, and the privatisation would be used to form the core of a French defence electronics sector.

The government quickly deviated from its own conditions to accommodate prospective bidder Lagardere, a publishing-to-missiles conglomerate. It had no interest in keeping TMM, which produces televisions and VCRs under the RCA, Saba, GE, Proscan and Telefunken brands.

The other bidder, engineering giant Alcatel Alsthom, agreed to bid for all of Thomson and was regarded as the likely winner. Its chances appeared to grow stronger after Lagardere lined up Daewoo to buy TMM.
The shock was palpable when Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced in October that the government had chosen Lagardere's bid.

He said it would pump 11 billion francs ($2.09 billion) into debt-saddled Thomson before selling it to Lagardere for "one symbolic franc". Lagardere in turn would sell TMM to Daewoo, also for one franc.
A surge in buying in Lagardere shares prior to the announcement reportedly triggered an investigation by the bourse regulator COB. But most people were taken aback.
"People were just pulling out their hair," Cohen said. "Why give TMM to Daewoo for one franc after a 10 billion franc recapitalisation? Daewoo had nothing to offer."
Thomson Multimedia workers poured into the streets to protest the sale, and Socialist opposition leaders lambasted the "fire sale" of TMM, with its valuable patents and technology.

But the government stood fast, explaining it favoured the creation of a defence giant through the merger of Lagardere's Matra missiles unit and Thomson's much larger Thomson-CSF defence electronics subsidiary.

French newspapers suggested Lagardere's victory was sealed by a secret note purporting to summarise an alleged conversation between the past and present bosses of Britain's GEC Plc, Alcatel's partner in GEC-Alsthom.

The note, whose existence has never been confirmed, alleged that Lord Weinstock and his successor, George Simpson, discussed the potential spoils from the privatisation of Thomson and Framatome, the state-owned nuclear reactor manufacturer proposed as a merger partner for GEC-Alsthom.
Weinstock said no such conversation took place but he believed a document existed. The French foreign ministry denied ever passing on such a report to President Chirac.
"This spy story made the decision-making process look even more detestable," said Cohen, adding the murkiness of the privatisation process had turned into a deep embarrassment.

"The government can't choose between Colbertism and capitalism and has chosen the weakest points of both systems," said Cohen, referring to 17th century minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert whose name is synonymous in France with state central planning.

Last month industrialist Jean-Luc Lagardere's handling of a 1992 merger between Matra and media group Hachette also came under the spotlight when a Paris magistrate opened an investigation. The probe was based on a Matra shareholder's allegation that he hid information. ($1=5.271 French Franc)
